transcript: Actually we are you know um settling the equivalent of the world GDP every [music] month. So if your clear stops for one day I mean the financial markets will face some trouble unfortunately. Hi everybody. I'm Nicolola Tangen, the CEO of the Norwegian Sovereign Wealth Fund. And today I'm talking to Valeri Oba, the CEO of Euroclair. Every time you buy a share or a bond, someone has to make sure the share actually moves and the money actually arrives. Most of us never think about it, but one company in Brussel does exactly that. And they do it for more than 1,000 trillion euros. That's also called a quadrillion. Now the company is Uroleair, the plumbing of global finance and my guest has spent more than 30 years at URL holding several positions before becoming the CEO. Welcome. >> Thank you very much. >> First of all, what so in your words, what does Eur do? >> I think you you explained it very well actually. We are a financial market infrastructure making sure that the funds you know move from where they are in the hands of investors to the um the hands of people who need fund in order to finance their project to finance their activity and so we are very much you know we have created this network between the issuer community and the investor community and we are doing that across different markets as well as different instruments. So >> so who are your clients? So the clients are basically all the financial institutions in the world. You know, we have about 3,500 clients and they are based in more than 80 markets. >> How do you make money? >> We make money through first of all, you know, the volatility of the markets. So we have a fee on the transaction. But then we also have safekeeping fees for all the assets under custody. And today we are holding 45 trillion of euros of assets under custody. And therefore this is you know we have uh safekeeping fees uh on those instruments. And the third source of revenues is net uh interest earnings. So basically whenever cash is left on our accounts um we invest the cash and we we earn net interest earnings. >> Who own you? We have a very uh interesting shareholder shareholdership in the sense that um it has changed and in the last five years it's stabilized and we have foreign um sovereign funds sorry like the sovereign fund of Belgium, sovereign fund of um uh Singapore. We also have very long-term investors such as the pension fund in New Zealand, pension fund in South um uh in um Australia. uh we have foundations and of course [clears throat] some of the banks as well. So it's a very diverse um shareholding which is reflecting a little bit the global footprint of Euro. >> So what would happen if you close for a day? >> Uh I think the news will not be good [laughter] because you know uh given the the role that we have for I mean across the market you were mentioning that actually we are you know um settling the equivalent of the world GDP every month. So if your clear stops for one day, I mean the financial markets will face some trouble unfortunately. >> Yeah. Yeah. Now uh settling trades is one of the things you do, but you also handle dividends, votes, corporate actions, uh what we uh in call asset servicing. So why does that matter? Well, it does it it does matter because when our clients are buying securities, they need to lodge them somewhere and then they need to make sure that throughout the life of the asset that they hold in their portfolio, you know, payment of dividends happen, corporate action happen. So the tax treatment also take place. So it's very important that we service the assets while they are in their wallets. What is also very important and I would say it's one of the key services that we have developed more recently it is al the collateral management because you know all these securities are sitting in a in a in a portfolio but they can be used to finance transactions you know so collateral management is um a service which is now really the glue I would say of your >> you mentioned that uh if you close for a day uh it would be a disaster so what is it that worries you post is it uh you know fraud cyber war >> well unfortunately for the time being the world is not going that well so there are quite a number of concerns but you're right the ones that you have me mentioned are important element especially I would say on the cyber um operational incident of course always exist as well at the same time you know we have a lot of um uh recovery capabilities we have you know I mean business continuity for us is really key uh in our agenda. It's also a key topic for the board. So hopefully we have you know we are equipped for this type of incident but you never know of course >> what are the kind of things you can do to protect. So you know we we are already in multiple locations both from an IT perspective. We have a number of data centers but you also have you know people who are located in different location and on a monthly basis we check or we test if you wish the move of the production from one place to the other to make sure that again we are able to really uh recover as quickly as possible. Otherwise you know we have also arrangement with our service providers to also you know smooth a number of things. So I mean yeah as I said business continuity is one of the top topic of the of the board of the management. >> In February 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine Russia central bank had almost 200 billion euros in securities sitting at euroclear. So what happened just after the invasion? So I mean at that time you know the international uh community decided to impose sanctions. So we had of course sanctions for the European uh authorities as well as from the US and other G7 countries and therefore of course I mean we implemented all these sanctions. So it meant that all the assets belonging to the central bank of Russia had been immobilized. Now the thing which happened as well is that those securities and usually when clients hold securities with us they are never part of the balance sheet of eurokle but over the time the securities redeemed and therefore were transformed into cash. Now euroclear has a banking status and therefore you know the cash started to fall on the balance sheet of euroclear and so now we have you know a balance sheet of almost 200 billion which is very much the result of this transformation from securities to cash >> what's going to happen with the cash >> so the cash for the time being is um invested by eurokar but at the same time contractually we can we never pay interest um on the cash which is left with us This is very much a demand from our regulators because given the systemic risk that we already have in terms of the securities business, our regulators wanted to make sure that we don't incentivize clients to also leave cash with us. So that's why for every client who is depositing cash with us, there is no remuneration. And of course, we apply the same rule for the sanctioned entities. And so um the cash which is sitting on our on our books is invested and all the revenues related to this investment of cash which is revenues belonging to euroclear all these revenues is paid back to the European authorities that's what we call the windfall contribution and I must say there the the board of euroclear the shareholders of euro clear have found that it was not opportune for euro clear to benefit from the war and that's why you know even So these are really purely benefits to Euro clear this is being given to the European Commission which is then you know using this money to support Ukraine. >> There's been a lot of discussion about this right >> there's been a lot of discussions because and I do understand >> and some people think you should take the 200 >> billion and give that as well to Ukraine >> and I really understand the emotions and the emotional aspect if you wish of this of that topic. I fully understand that and as a citizen I have my my own beliefs as a CEO of Eurocar I need also to make sure that the decision makers understand the unintended consequences of such a decision because there is a legal regime which is very specific to the assets belonging to a state and so far you know according to this special legal regime there is no um opportunity there is no legal you know um reasons to seize those assets. Second thing which is also very important is not only um about um seizing the assets but it is also about continuing to provide confidence in the European markets. You know the European markets for 60 years benefit from a very strong credibility because of the legal certainty, the respect of the rule of law. I mean this is also um you know allowing so many foreign investors to continue to invest in Europe. But clearly if we start completely um eroding the trust of those investors into the markets by changing the rules and by not respecting the rule of law that could certainly deter some of those investors from the European markets and so that's also a consequence that we have to pay attention to. >> When you look at uh Europe relative to the US uh in the US you have one big settlement system in Europe you have many. How does that uh how does that impact Europe you think? [sighs] Well, you know, it depends a little bit what you are looking and in Europe, we always tend to look at it what does not work and we forget what works well, right? So there is a history in Europe and we are not the United States of Europe. We continue to be a number of countries with all its uh market practices. But still when you look at um you know the the volumes in in Europe, there has there has always been already been a integration or consolidation of the markets. You know when you take euro clear and clear we already represent more than 90% of the volumes um you know u managed settle set settled in in European assets. Euro clear alone will represent 50% of all the European assets. So we already had seen some consolidation also because both Euro clear stream and now Euronex have also started to acquire a number of CSD. So there has already been a form of integration. Now it is true that when you really zoom into the instrument you know euro bonds very uh integrated only between your clear and clear stream. You you look at the fixed income in Europe pretty integrated thanks as well to the collateral management because collateral management is a is a service which allows for you know pooling of assets. Now ETFs for example very also integrated but fair to say that the uh equities remain a market which is fragmented and it is fragmented also because every country is its own corporate law its own uh laws in terms of bankruptcy in terms of taxes etc and so you're right that unfortunately despite the fact that few groups own a number of CSDs still the equity market is fragmented. Do you think we'll see um capital markets union in Europe? >> I'm an optimistic person, so I really hope that we will see some progress. >> But if you have to put on your realistic hat, >> I think it will un I'm I'm I'm doubt that it will be done very fast. And also when you look at what is happening in Europe with also I mean there is a very heavy election agenda in the coming 18 months >> and these are always moments where you know there is more focus on domestic uh interests rather than on European ones. So I must say that um I fear that it will take maybe longer than what we are all expecting. >> How do you see Euroair as a bridge between Asia and Europe? Well, it's a very important for for me. It's really part of the of the strategic uh priorities of Euroclair. I mean, Eurokair always had um you know a strong uh commercial footprint in Asia. So, we are we have long-standing relationship with Asian investors, but we want to continue to increase it and we want to continue to increase it for different reasons. So, first of all, it's a it's a continent where the growth is higher than in Europe. So, I think it's important to be part of it. But we also saw some changes in the behaviors of the investors. You know initially the investors were primarily invested in the US and then eventually you know investing in other parts of the world and while doing when they were investing outside their country and the US usually they were using um a westerner counterparty you know um an agent or custodian or now we see that there are more and more investment flows within Asia. So you know um I don't know Japan investing in Singapore, Singaporean investing in Australia you know so we see that there are more and more investment flows within the APAC region and Euro clear we have really built this knowledge of um uh bridging different pools of assets you know bringing interoperability between the different markets and therefore we believe that we can also play a role within the Asian region by continuing to share prepare, you know, our expertise um for the Asian markets. And so, yes, definitely Asia and continuing to build links with Asia also between Asia and Middle East is something that is part of the um delivery on which we are working. >> Changing tax a bit here, how do you think AI will change your business? >> Well, AI is already changing the business, you know. Um I mean AI certainly internally is already changing the business in the sense that we are using AI more and more to improve efficiency and um and and I believe and and I and I continue really to to insist that AI should be seen by many of us like an opportunity you know it's a way to reduce the um uh the manual tasks to get to to have better information and therefore to uh eventually increase the um the value that we can bring to our clients. So clearly AI is being used a lot in operations but also in IT to improve um or to modernize our our IT IT stack. And we are also starting now to use AI to develop more services for our clients. >> Another technology which is impacting you is uh tokenization. >> Uh and I believe you're working with bank France to tokenize the uh part of the the short-term debt market. just um explain please tokenization what is it? Yeah. Well, tokenization is basically representing in fractions, you know, an asset. Um, and um, I I have a I am a strong believer in this program that we are working on with Bong the France because, you know, so far DT works, but in the capital markets there has not been really a winning, you know, uh, a winning initiative in the sense that the market adoption remains very slow and very low. And so um we have we have seen in in you know some of experimentation that issuers can come but there there are not enough benefits for really uh investor to to to join the initiative. >> Can blockchain actually replace your business you think? >> No I don't think so and I think that's something that we were talking a lot about five years ago. You know there was a comment that everybody will be disintermediated. I think there is again our recognition that having a trusted uh party and also a neutral party will be important to avoid fragmentation. You know typically Euro clear we can work with everybody. Now if it is a a platform which is developed by HSBC or by city bank or by BNP Bara their competitors will not join the counter the the platform you know. So that's why having uh somebody like Eurokle which has this neutrality but also um this um this knowledge you know and the trust I think it's something that is being still valued by the by the players in the capital market and so PGO because that's the name of the initiative is really working with a full ecosystem to migrate it you know in one go on the on the on the on the blockchain and so Bong de France is providing the cash leg with the use case of the first use case of digital euro. So that's uh you know that probably you have heard about the the the project pontest in ECB and so that is one of the first use case of uh of ECB of pontest and we are providing the securities leg and we are really working with the issuer the traders the primary dealers the investors to you know adopt the new technology and I'm sure that we will learn plenty of things there >> in the US they've had stable coins for a long time uh is digital euro a bit late >> it depends on the need you know I think that for the the type of business that we have uh it is not too late it's uh and it makes a lot of sense I think for the retail market uh on which I'm not really part of probably that stable coins is something which is also attractive uh for for the retail and there are some opportunities which are emerging in Europe you know so we'll have to see how it it evolves yeah >> you mentioned the um the expression t plus one and it basically the amount of days it take to settle a trade right So um in the US they changed to one day settlement in 2024. In Europe it will happen from October next year. >> Yeah. >> Um why does it still take two days in Europe when it can go much faster? Well, you know, when we talk about T+1 or T plus0, I mean, you have to realize that is not just, you know, on the platform of Euro clear that this is happening because actually today we can already do T plus Z and we have a number of sophisticated clients who are using this functionality. But what you have to realize is that when we talk about you know uh I don't know an investor a retail investor buying securities on the stock exchange usually has to go to give an instruction to its bank the bank to first probably to his broker then the broker to the bank then the bank to us then the bank you know so there is a long chain of intervening parties and so the more you reduce the time between the trading and the settlement the more this chain needs to be very effective and very quick you know in giving instruction for the information to flow from one side to the other. >> Do you think it will be instant at some stage? >> No, I don't think so. I don't think well I have to um I have to to to nuance um I think that there could already as I as it is the case today for very very sophisticated operations or for you know um maybe snap um retail you may have you know some of that but I don't think that in the institutional business this will happen and the reason I'm saying that as well is that um again I was referring to the Asian markets. When the Asian investors invest in Europe, they usually do that from their head office, you know, from Japan, from China, from, you know, all their countries. While when they invest in in the US, usually they do that from their US location, from their US office. And so they are in the same time zone. Europe, you know, T+1 in Europe means T plus Z for the Asian investors because of the time zone difference. So I think that if you want again to continue to attract you know investors from all around the world you need also to take into consideration this reality and that's why I believe that from a wholesale uh business I don't see t plus zero happening across the board. It will happen for some specific operations for sure but not for the the the usual transactions. [snorts] >> I'd love to uh talk a bit about leadership. You joined Euroclair in 1992. What would you say is the biggest change in the company since you joined apart from of course you becoming the CEO? >> Well, many things have changed because when I was when I started I remember that uh we had no um Blackberry, we had no emails. I was I remember that I was still uh you know typing my letters to the clients. So the speed um the speed of interaction has changed dramatically. um the sophistication of the markets therefore has changed dramatically. The usage of new technology so lots of things have changed actually. >> Who's been the most important person in your life as a leader? Well, I have had very generous bo uh bosses, you know, bosses who have really um pushed me outside my comfort zone and I have in mind uh somebody who who you when when you I was meeting him, you you knew when you were entering in his in his office, but you never knew knew when you would get out because you know he will always use any interaction as a learning opportunity, you know, and really forcing you to find yourself the the answer to your question and Um I found that having this kind of boss is extremely um uh educative but also it it builds your self-confidence you know. So yeah and I I have one in mind but I also have others who who have had this generosity to each time you know continues to push me uh and and and support me as well in the um in in the the progression. >> How do you work in supporting the people who are coming after you? Well, it's very much by uh listening also by challenging them um by and then when when I I have I I'm trusting them, you know, it's really to expose them and to give them the opportunity to to do things by their own. So, yeah, I think it's a it's it's it's an art. It's not it's not a science. And you need also to adapt your style to the people that you have in front of you because not everybody requires the same support. And so that's why really listening and trying to understand um where the person is is extremely important. For some people you will need to be positively encouraging them. For others you will need to challenge them. So um yeah as I said it's a it's an art but it is certainly one of the things that um you know nourished me the most. >> You led in a period with a you know war a lot of uncertainty technology change. What do you think is the key to being a good leader in in a period of so much change? >> I think to remain authentic and to share the good news and the bad news. You know um I've seen that last year when we were in the middle of the discussion on the Russian assets. you know, I've been extremely open with my uh I mean with with with my staff, you know, explaining when it was uh starting to become sensitive, not sensitive, you know, and I think that um that has created a lot of trust also between me and the staff. So remaining authentic because um we are not superman, superwoman. We we have our own vulnerabilities and that's a way also to recognize that the value of the team you know it's not a one man or one woman show it is about um engaging all the all your your colleagues to really drive and accept changes. I think this is the most difficult thing for me is making people accept changes because unfortunately the change uh is becoming constant and >> do you like do you like change? >> I do because otherwise I don't think I will be where I am. So yes, I do like the change even though sometimes it's tiring but uh yeah, I think that's also what keeps you energetic and it's a way also to con constantly learn actually. >> Absolutely. I love I love change. Um now when you look at the people around you how would you how would you characterize the copa culture at Yorklair? >> Well you know I always say that I stayed for more than 30 years because of the people and um we have um on one side we we are very much expert in our domain and we like to you know to show our expertise but it remains a um I mean a human company. We are only 6,000 people um and so there is still a human touch which for me is extremely important. So yes, we are demanding but at the same time um we are caring also about people. Um sometimes you know I would like that we are even more performing and that's the things that I'm also bringing because u uh the market is not easier the the competition is not quieter. So it's important that we remain on top of but I still like very much this uh ability to care about people and to talk about people. M h what failure has uh changed you the most in life? What have you what's been your biggest failure? >> Well, I think failures um well first of all you know I love Mandela and Mandela has always said there is no failure. Either you win or you learn and that's something that I've tried to apply throughout my life. Um you know failure is probably when I lost an RFP you know I lost a business to to my competition. And so this is the type of things where you start requesting yourself and requesting the way of positioning um the company. At the end of the day, what matters is what you learn about you and about our capability to overcome this um difficult period. >> You were born and raised in Sagal. >> Do you [laughter] do you think that um helped create this resilience in some way, shape or form? In what ways? Definitely because first of all I think that it taught me um the the value of the differences you know uh I was a different uh I was not from from Sineagal and so I was different since I was very very young and so I think you you nurture therefore the value of having diversity in people with different background people with different u perspectives. So certainly that has I mean my my youth because I traveled a lot uh in different uh African countries and that has really taught me that. Um I think also because um at a certain point of time I had to come back to to Belgium you know when I was 16 years old and to live on my own because my parents continue their expat life. Um I mean when you are alone at 16 years old there are moments which are great but there are moments which are very lonely and again I mean you you need to overcome these kind of shortcomings. >> Is there anything from your African upbringing that you have brought with you? Yeah, I think well first of all this diversity and inclusion for sure but also this capability of taking um the moment in in a joyful way you know I think um African lives in the in the moment and I think I try to always be very present at the moment we are in >> do you meditate >> no I don't [laughter] you just talk about being being in the moment right uh >> exactly no I don't meditate [laughter] >> are you a spir are you a spiritual Uh I am somehow yes I have my um my own beliefs and yeah but I think this is also probably something that I took a little bit from Africa. >> So yeah definitely >> what's something about you that most people don't know. [laughter] >> Well now it's not a secret anymore in Euroc but it is a secret outside you know I'm I'm collecting the Smurfves. The Smurfs you know that's a little Belgian character you know. So yeah so I continued with that. So that's that's something which is uh which I had to reveal when I became CEO of Yok and it's very nice because I have now people uh you know um offering me uh some smurs. >> How many how many do you have? >> Oh it's not 300. >> Okay. [laughter] [gasps] >> Um when do you get up in the morning? >> 6:00. >> How do you relax? >> Reading. >> What do you read? >> Certainly not professional books. I have to switch off and usually I read in French because um you know the the French literature I mean listening to French because Brit English is my uh professional uh um language and so I I really like to I really enjoy reading French Romans also history historical books I like that. >> What's the um what's the book that has given you the most? Well, there are so many um there is one book which I always uh go back to is Libertango. So, it's about you know a conductor of um of music. So, I mean and you could I mean the the the writer has written the book while listening to music and when you read it it's almost as if you listen to the music. >> And what kind of music do you listen to? >> I love blues. I love jazz and otherwise, you know, I'm pretty uh eclectic in in music. >> Lastly, what is your advice to young people? >> For young people, do what what um I mean um you know, work with your passion. I mean, you we spend so much time at work. You need to really enjoy it. And the second point is believe in yourself because plenty of people will tell you shouldn't do this, you shouldn't do that. believe in yourself because often I feel in the new generation that there is not always sufficient self-confidence and uh I think they are also there to manage the future of our companies and so we also need to listen to them we also need to learn from them and to see how we can prepare them for becoming the future leaders and so I mean um we need to trust them they need to trust themselves and to believe in them in themselves. M m great place to end and um thank you for all your hard work. We for sure trust you a lot because you settle millions and millions of our trades every year and so for that a big thank you to you and the team and uh we look forward to staying in touch. >> Thank you very much and thank you for your interest. [music] >> Thank you. Really hoped you liked the episode. If you did, please like it, subscribe, and put on the notification. This really helps us to get new great guests.
